topics.title: Levels of Prevention, Care Settings & What Shapes Care
topics.summary: Sort every nursing action by its goal—prevent, find early, or restore—and spot the life factors that decide whether care actually reaches the client.
objectives: You can sort any nursing action into primary, secondary, or tertiary prevention.
You can tell care settings apart from prevention levels.
You can pick the safest, least costly care setting.
You can explain how demographics, SDOH, and ACEs shape health.
You can use technology safely and check the client can use it.
You can spot low health literacy and use teach-back.
topics.bigPicture:
A healthcare system is more than a hospital. It is all the people, places, money, and resources that deliver care. That includes care given locally, statewide, nationally, and worldwide. You work inside this system every shift. Many bedside choices are really system choices. Is this the right place for this client? Will money, housing, or reading skills block the plan at home?

The NCLEX rarely asks you to define a term. It shows a nurse doing something and asks which level of prevention it is. Or it hides a barrier, like a client who “forgot my glasses,” and asks what to do. This lesson gives you one question to sort prevention. It also teaches the cues that reveal hidden barriers.
recap: Prevention level depends on the target condition and whether the client already has it—never on the building.
Primary prevents disease. Secondary finds it early. Tertiary restores function and quality of life.
Screenings and self-exams are secondary. A vaccine is primary, even for a chronically ill client.
Primary, secondary, and tertiary care are places. Prevention levels are goals.
Choose the least costly setting that safely meets the need.
SDOH and ACEs drive many poor outcomes. Assess the barrier and refer; do not blame the client.
Technology helps only with nursing judgment and a client who can use it.
You cannot see low health literacy. Use plain language and teach-back with everyone.

keyTerms.def: All the people, places, payment methods, and resources that deliver and manage care—locally, statewide, nationally, and internationally.
Care for healthy people that keeps disease from starting, such as vaccines, healthy-habit teaching, prenatal care, and lead removal.
Finding disease early and treating it fast so it does not progress: screenings, self-exams, risk checks, and (in this course) preventing hospital complications.
Care after disease is established, stable, or incurable. It restores function, limits complications, and protects quality of life. Includes rehab and palliative care.
WHO (1986): helping people gain control over and improve their health. It prevents disease instead of treating it.
The entry point to care: offices, clinics, community health centers, schools, and health fairs.
Hospitals, outpatient surgery centers, and specialists’ offices, usually reached by referral.
Highly specialized care in hospitals, rehab centers, and extended care facilities.
Conditions where people are born, live, learn, work, play, and age that affect their health. Healthy People 2030 groups them into five domains.
Possibly traumatic events from birth through age 17, such as abuse, neglect, or a jailed parent. They raise adult risk of chronic disease, mental illness, STIs, and suicide.
The ability to get through change or trauma with little long-term harm. Communities build it through safe, stable, caring relationships and support.
Care that assumes any client may have a trauma history. It stresses safety, choice, teamwork, and empowerment.
The ability to get, share, process, and understand basic health information to make good choices. Includes print, oral, number, and technology skills.
Asking the client to explain or show what you taught, in their own words. It checks your teaching, not the client’s intelligence.
Communicating clearly with every client, because you cannot tell by looking who struggles to understand.
Giving care or monitoring clients from a distance by electronic communication. It needs a device, internet, and tech skills.
A digital, shareable health record that supports coordination, decision-support alerts, and barcode medication scanning.

sections.heading: What are the three levels of prevention?
sections.keyIdea: Name the target condition, then ask one question: does the client already have it?
sections.body:
The levels of prevention describe the goal of a nursing action. The goal depends on the client’s disease status right now. It never depends on the building.

Name the target condition first. Then ask if the client has it yet. A flu shot for a client with COPD is still primary. The target is the flu, and the client does not have it.

One shortcut always works. A screening test or self-exam is secondary. Its job is to find disease, not stop it.
bullets: Primary — prevent it. The client is healthy. Vaccines, healthy-habit teaching, quit-smoking help, prenatal care, job safety, sanitation, lead removal, food access.
Secondary — find it early. Disease may be silent. Risk checks, BP and vision screenings, teaching self-exams.
Secondary — limit an acute problem (course rule). Carry out the acute care plan. Prevent hospital complications like pressure injury and DVT.
Tertiary — restore and protect. Disease is established or incurable. Ostomy nurse, dietitian for complications, pain specialist, PT, rehab, palliative care.

rows: New hypertension client taught to take the pill
Turning a postop client every 2 hours
Daily weights for heart failure; cardiac rehab

check.q: A nurse teaches healthy teens the testicular self-exam. Why is this secondary, not primary?
check.a: A self-exam cannot stop cancer from forming. It finds cancer early, while it is treatable. A vaccine that prevents disease, like HPV vaccine, is primary.

sections.heading: Is primary care the same as primary prevention?
sections.keyIdea: Care settings are places; prevention levels are goals. Every setting can deliver all three levels.
sections.body:
The words primary, secondary, and tertiary also name care settings. This overlap is a classic trap. A setting tells you where care happens. A prevention level tells you what the care is trying to do. One office visit can hold all three levels.

A key nursing job is picking the most cost-effective setting. In the course example, a small basal cell carcinoma is removed under local anesthesia in a dermatologist’s office. The outcome matches the hospital OR, at lower cost and with less disruption.
bullets: Primary care: the entry point. Offices, clinics, community health centers, schools, churches, malls, health fairs. Checkups, vaccines, common illness, emotional support.
Secondary care: hospitals, outpatient surgery centers, specialists’ offices, usually by referral.
Tertiary care: hospitals, rehab centers, extended care facilities for complex care. The nurse advocates, coordinates, and promotes following the plan.
Other settings (Figure 46.1): ED, flight transport, OR, NICU, schools, public health, home health, prisons, insurers, universities, publishing.
sections.analogy: Settings are floors in a building. Prevention levels are jobs done on every floor. The floor tells you where you are. The job tells you what you are trying to do.

check.q: At a family practice office, a healthy adult gets a Tdap vaccine. Name the setting and the level.
check.a: Setting: primary care. Level: primary prevention, because the client does not have tetanus, diphtheria, or pertussis. Same word, two meanings.

sections.heading: How are people and technology changing care?
sections.keyIdea: An older, more diverse population needs more chronic care, and technology is safe only with nursing judgment.
sections.body:
Demographics means the makeup of the population. By 2060 the U.S. will be older and more diverse. Adults 85 and older will more than triple, from about 6 million to about 19 million. They often have several chronic illnesses.

By 2030, nearly half of U.S. adults may have obesity, and about one in four severe obesity. Women, non-Hispanic Black adults, and homes earning under $50,000 are hit hardest.

Technology supports judgment but never replaces it. A scanner cannot tell you a dose is unsafe with today’s potassium.
bullets: Aging: more home health, long-term care, rehab, palliative care, and caregiver teaching.
Obesity: more diabetes and heart disease, so stress prevention and screening.
Diversity: professional interpreters and culturally responsive care.
EHR and barcoding: scan wristband and drug at the bedside. Check flagged labs first. No taped barcode copies, no overriding alerts to save time. Report scanner failures.
Minimally invasive surgery: shorter stays, so start discharge teaching early.
Telehealth: helps rural clients only with a device, internet, privacy, and skills.

check.q: A rural client is offered cardiology follow-up by video. What should the nurse check first?
check.a: A working device, home internet, privacy, and the skills to use it. Otherwise telehealth becomes another barrier.

sections.heading: What are social determinants of health?
sections.keyIdea: When a plan fails, look for a life barrier before you call the client nonadherent.
sections.body:
Medical care is only part of health. The rest comes from social determinants of health (SDOH): where people are born, live, learn, work, play, and age. Healthy People 2030 sorts them into five domains.

On the NCLEX, cues hide in the social history: “works two jobs,” “rides the bus,” “ran out of insulin before payday.” The best answer names the barrier and links the client to help. Nonadherence is a label. An SDOH barrier is often the real cause.

rows: Ask about cost; social work; assistance programs
Lives alone; no ride after a procedure
No primary provider; uses the ED

check.q: A client with heart failure is readmitted. He says, “I can’t afford the scale and I don’t have a ride to the clinic.” Best action?
check.a: Refer to case management or social work for a scale and rides, and arrange home health or telemonitoring. Do not just repeat daily-weight teaching.

sections.heading: What are ACEs, and what builds resiliency?
sections.keyIdea: ACEs raise lifelong health risk, but caring adults and community supports build resiliency that softens the harm.
sections.body:
Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are possibly traumatic events from birth to age 17. Examples are abuse, neglect, seeing violence, a parent with addiction or mental illness, divorce, or a jailed family member.

About two-thirds of U.S. adults report at least one ACE. About one in six report four or more. Toxic stress changes the growing brain and immune system. So ACEs raise adult risk for heart disease, diabetes, depression, substance use, STIs, and suicide.

Resiliency is the hopeful half: getting through trauma with little lasting harm. Communities build it with caring adults and support.
steps: Ask about stress and safety in private, with calm, nonjudging words.
Check for current danger. Suspected abuse is reported to the child protective agency—no investigating, no waiting for proof.
Build protective factors: home visits and parenting help, a steady adult mentor, food aid, child care.
Refer early. Never tell a child to keep family problems secret.
Use trauma-informed care: explain, offer choices, protect privacy.
sections.example: A 15-year-old has frequent headaches. Her father was just jailed, and she cares for her brothers at night. The nurse screens for depression and safety and links her to the school counselor.

sections.heading: What is health literacy?
sections.keyIdea: You cannot see low health literacy, so use plain language and teach-back with every client.
sections.body:
Health literacy is the ability to get, share, and understand basic health information to make good choices. It has four parts, listed below.

Only about 53% of U.S. adults have intermediate health literacy. About 36% have basic or below-basic skills. Low health literacy leads to medication errors, more hospital stays, and more deaths.

You cannot judge it by looks or schooling. So speak clearly to everyone, and use teach-back.
bullets: Print: reading and writing. Oral: listening and speaking.
Numeracy: doses, times, glucose values. Technology: portals and apps.
Warning cues: “forgot my glasses,” takes forms home, blank forms, names pills by color, missed visits.
steps: Use plain words: “high blood pressure,” not “hypertension.”
Teach 2–3 key points, safety first.
Demonstrate. Check numeracy with a real task, like showing the dose on a syringe.
Ask: “Tell me how you will take this tomorrow morning.” Re-teach a new way if needed.
Use a professional interpreter, not family. Written sheets back up, never replace, teaching.

check.q: After insulin teaching, a client says, “I understand,” but hands back the sheet unread. What next?
check.a: Treat it as a literacy cue. Have him show how he draws up and gives the dose, and explain what to do for low blood sugar.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes on prevention and barriers
sections.keyIdea: Most errors come from reacting to one word—name the target condition and the real goal first.
sections.body: Use the clue in the right column.

rows: A goal (keep disease away) vs a place (office, clinic).
Stops disease from starting vs finds it. Screens and self-exams are secondary.
Early or acute problem vs established disease. Rehab and palliative = tertiary.
Vaccine for a chronically ill client
Still primary. Name the infection, not the other diagnoses.
No. Ask what disease the teaching targets.
Health literacy adds numbers and tech. Graduates misread doses too.
Barrier is the cause; fix it with a referral.
Risk exposure vs protection from caring adults and programs.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Label every option primary, secondary, or tertiary, then pick the one that matches what the stem asks.
sections.body: Expect a few common patterns. Each one tests whether you can name the goal of an action or spot a hidden barrier.
bullets: Classify: “Which action is tertiary prevention?” or “Which statement needs more teaching?”
Barrier spotting: SDOH or literacy cues; the answer fixes the barrier.
Safety first: BP 186/118 with severe headache at a health fair means activate emergency care.
sections.example: Sample question: A neighborhood has high hypertension rates, many adults with no primary provider, and no grocery store. Which intervention is secondary prevention? A. Partner with a farmers’ market to accept food benefits. B. Free BP screenings at a church health fair. C. A walking club for healthy residents. D. Refer stroke survivors to rehab.
steps: Read the stem: it asks for SECONDARY prevention, not the best program overall.
What is it asking? An action that finds disease early.
Key cues: high hypertension rates and no provider suggest many people have undiagnosed hypertension.
A is wrong: food access prevents disease (primary). C is wrong: exercise for healthy people is primary. D is wrong: rehab restores function (tertiary).
The answer is B. Screening finds hypertension before stroke.
Strategy: write P, S, or T beside each option, then pick the label the stem asks for.

sections.heading: Worked case: one clinic visit, three levels
sections.keyIdea: Sort each need by prevention level, but handle the most dangerous problem first.
sections.body: Mr. Alvarez, 58, comes to a community health center after an ED visit for high blood pressure. He works nights, takes two buses, has no regular provider, and has smoked 30 years. BP today is 168/98 mm Hg. He never read his discharge paper, has never had colorectal screening, and limps from an old knee injury.
steps: Cues: high BP, no usual source of care, smoker, overdue screening, money and transport barriers, possible literacy gap.
Sort: primary = quit-smoking help, vaccines. Secondary = BP follow-up, colorectal screening. Tertiary = knee PT to prevent falls.
Prioritize the BP. Recheck it and ask about headache, vision change, chest pain, and weakness. Make sure the provider treats it today.
Fix barriers: sliding-fee and transport help, and this clinic as his medical home.
Teach two plain points, then use teach-back.

check.q: Which need is tertiary, and why does it wait?
check.a: Knee physical therapy is tertiary—it restores function. The uncontrolled BP carries the most immediate risk of stroke, so it comes first.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, anyone who suspects child maltreatment must report it to county DSS—suspicion is enough.
bullets: Universal reporting (G.S. 7B-301): anyone who suspects a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent, or died from maltreatment, must report to the county DSS director.
Report suspicion. Do not investigate or wait for proof. Knowingly failing to report is a crime; good-faith reporters are immune.
Disabled adults (G.S. 108A-102): anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to county DSS, orally or in writing. Good-faith reporters are immune.

Telehealth: NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. An RN with a multistate license (NC as home state) may give telehealth across compact states and follows the laws of the state where the client is. The NC Board of Nursing regulates practice (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Module 46 study guide, outcomes 46.1–46.2; textbook pp. 2773–2777 (Table 46.1, Figure 46.1). Cases and walkthroughs are original.
ACEs: the course says “about 1 in 6 children.” CDC: about 64% of adults report at least one ACE; about 1 in 6 report four or more. So “1 in 6” means high exposure (4+ ACEs), not overall prevalence.
“Pressure ulcer” is now pressure injury (NPIAP).
The course calls preventing hospital complications secondary because an acute illness exists. Some texts say primary. Follow the course and reason from the target condition.
Teach-back, universal precautions, and trauma-informed care were added as standard practice.

mnemonics.name: P-S-T = Prevent, Spot, Tune-up
mnemonics.text: Primary PREVENTS disease (vaccines, healthy habits). Secondary SPOTS it early (screenings, self-exams). Tertiary TUNES UP function after disease is established (rehab, referrals, palliative care).

mnemonics.name: Four health literacies: “PONT”
mnemonics.text: Print (read and write), Oral (listen and speak), Numeracy (doses, numbers), Technology (portals, apps). A gap in any one can derail the plan.

pearls: Classify prevention by the target condition—never by the setting.
Rehab, complication referrals, and palliative care are tertiary.
“I understand” is not proof of learning. Use teach-back or return demonstration.
When a plan fails, look for an SDOH barrier before labeling nonadherence.
Pick the office procedure over the hospital OR when it is equally safe.
redFlags: A client cannot show how to use insulin or an anticoagulant before discharge. Do not discharge on teaching alone; escalate and re-teach.
Signs of current child abuse or neglect. Report the suspicion to child protective services; do not investigate first.
High BP with severe headache, vision change, chest pain, or neuro deficits at a screening. Activate emergency care.
A client rationing medicine because of cost. Notify the provider and involve social work.

checks.q: A home health nurse teaches a client recovering from hip replacement to use a walker and remove throw rugs. Which level of prevention is this?
checks.a: Tertiary. The hip problem is established. The teaching restores function and prevents falls.

checks.q: A community has high rates of undiagnosed diabetes. A health fair nurse can offer glucose screening or diabetes-prevention nutrition classes. Which is secondary, and why might it be the better choice here?
checks.a: Glucose screening is secondary. It finds existing disease so treatment starts before complications. Nutrition classes are primary and do not find disease.

checks.q: A parent in an older rental home asks why the clinic wants to test her toddler’s blood lead level. How does lead fit the levels of prevention?
checks.a: Removing lead from housing is primary. Testing the child’s blood lead is secondary—it finds exposure early.

checks.q: A teen with several ACEs is close to her soccer coach and attends an after-school program. How should the nurse view these findings?
checks.a: They are protective factors that build resiliency. Support them, and still screen for current safety.

checks.q: A new graduate says, “I can usually tell which clients need simpler teaching from their education level.” Is this correct?
checks.a: No. Health literacy cannot be judged by schooling or looks. Use plain language and teach-back with everyone.

topics.title: Models of Care, Insurance & Access to Care
topics.summary: Tell managed care, case management, and patient-focused care apart, and spot the barriers that keep clients from care—plus the safety nets that help.
objectives: You can tell managed care, case management, and patient-focused care apart.
You can compare HMOs and PPOs and explain the gatekeeper.
You can pick the client who most needs a case manager.
You can match a client to Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, or a sliding-fee clinic.
You can apply EMTALA in the emergency department.
You can name access barriers and the nurse’s response to each.
topics.bigPicture:
Two clients leave the hospital with the same diagnosis and prescriptions. One stays well. The other is back in the ED in a week. Often the difference is access: insurance that covers the drug, a provider to see next week, a clinic close enough to reach, and knowing when a symptom is an emergency.

This lesson covers how care is organized and paid for, and what blocks clients from getting it. On the NCLEX, these ideas appear as discharge, referral, and “best response” items. The right answer protects safety first. Then it teaches and links the client to the right program.
recap: Managed care = cost and quality for groups. Case management = connected care for one complex client. Patient-focused care = client’s needs lead.
HMO: gatekeeper referral, lower cost. PPO: self-referral, higher cost.
Refer the client with the most complex coordination needs to the case manager.
Access has three steps: entry, a site with the service, and a trusted provider.
Uninsured means no coverage. Underinsured means coverage that falls short.
Medicare: 65+ or disability. Medicaid: low income. CHIP: kids above Medicaid limits.
EMTALA: emergency screening and stabilization or proper transfer, regardless of ability to pay.
Meet ED overuse with respectful teaching and a medical home.

keyTerms.def: Cost-effective, high-quality care for groups of members through provider networks. Main types: HMOs and PPOs.
A restrictive plan: network providers only, gatekeeper referral for specialists, no out-of-network coverage except emergencies, lower cost.
A flexible plan: self-referral and out-of-network care allowed, with higher premiums, copays, and deductibles.
The primary care provider in managed care who coordinates care and approves referrals to specialists.
Premium: regular payment for coverage. Copay: fixed fee at a visit. Deductible: what you pay each year before the plan pays.
A team process of assessing, planning, coordinating, evaluating, and advocating to meet a client’s full needs safely and cost-effectively.
A nurse, social worker, or other team member who coordinates care for clients with complex needs.
Smooth, connected care across providers, settings, and time, so the plan follows the client.
Care organized around the client’s stated physical and emotional needs, with client and family as partners.
Three steps: get into the system, reach a site with the service, and find a provider the client can trust.
Having no health coverage at all—public, employer, or private.
Having coverage that does not meet one’s needs, such as a plan that excludes a needed drug or a child’s vaccines.
Federal law that expanded coverage and barred denial for preexisting conditions in compliant plans.
A regular provider or clinic. It builds trust, improves prevention, and lowers costs. Over 40 million Americans lack one.
A primary care model built on the six principles in Box 46.2.
Federal insurance for adults 65+ and people with qualifying disabilities or diseases, such as end-stage renal disease.
Federal–state coverage for low-income people. It covers long-term custodial nursing home care. Medicare covers only short-term skilled nursing care.
Children’s Health Insurance Program: covers children whose families earn too much for Medicaid but cannot afford private insurance.
Charges based on income, used by health departments and community health centers.
Federal law: hospitals in Medicare with emergency services must screen anyone seeking emergency care and stabilize or properly transfer them, regardless of ability to pay.
The client’s own sense of how urgent a symptom is.
Providers spread unevenly: rural areas lack specialists; cities may face poverty and language barriers.
Preventable differences in disease or access to care faced by disadvantaged groups.

sections.heading: What are the three frameworks of care?
sections.keyIdea: Managed care is about money for groups, case management is about connecting one client’s care, and patient-focused care is about the client’s wishes.
sections.body:
The course names three frameworks. Each answers a different question, which is the fastest way to tell them apart. They often overlap in one client. On the exam, decide which framework one specific action shows.

Patient-focused care does not mean doing anything asked, even if unsafe. The competent client decides. Family are partners when the client wants them. If a wish conflicts with safety, explore why, explain the risk, and offer options.

rows: How do we give a group good care at a fair cost?
How do we keep one complex client’s care connected?
Arranging services and follow-up across settings
Schedule or plan built around the client’s request; family included

sections.example: A client on chemotherapy says morning visits make him too sick to drive. Patient-focused: his infusion moves to the afternoon, and his wife joins teaching. Case management: rides are arranged on bad days. Managed care: his plan requires prior approval for an antinausea drug.

check.q: A nurse schedules dressing teaching in the evening so the client’s spouse, who works days, can attend, as the client asked. Which framework is this?
check.a: Patient-focused care. The plan is built around the client’s stated needs, with family as partners.

sections.heading: How do HMOs and PPOs differ?
sections.keyIdea: An HMO trades choice for lower cost and needs a gatekeeper referral; a PPO trades higher cost for freedom.
sections.body:
Managed care plans aim for cost-effective, high-quality care for groups. The two main types differ in restriction versus cost.

Plan type changes discharge. An HMO client needs a primary care referral to see a specialist. “Just call any cardiologist” could mean a denied claim. A PPO client going out of network should know it costs more. The nurse teaches how the plan works and involves the case manager, but never promises coverage.
sections.example: An HMO client leaves with new atrial fibrillation and orders to see cardiology in a week. The nurse involves the case manager to get the referral before discharge.

check.q: An HMO client asks, “Can I just call the lung specialist my neighbor uses?” What should the nurse explain?
check.a: In an HMO, the primary care provider is the gatekeeper. The client needs a referral for the specialist visit to be covered, except in emergencies.

sections.heading: What does a case manager do?
sections.keyIdea: Case management keeps complex care connected across hospital, community, and home, and it begins at admission.
sections.body:
In case management, a case manager sits at the center of the team. That may be a nurse, social worker, or other team member. The goal is continuity of care across hospital, community, and home.

Who needs it most? Clients with complex, multi-provider needs: several chronic illnesses, frequent readmissions, new home equipment, little support, or big SDOH barriers. Pick the client with the most coordination needs, not just the sickest one.

Discharge planning starts on admission. The case manager coordinates but does not replace the nurse’s assessment.
steps: Assess health, function, support, insurance, SDOH, and the client’s goals.
Plan measurable goals with the client, family, and team.
Facilitate and coordinate services, equipment, referrals, and follow-up across settings.
Advocate for options and services, including appealing denials.
Evaluate outcomes such as readmissions, function, and cost, then revise the plan.

check.q: Which client most needs the case manager: a healthy adult after appendectomy, a teen with a sprain, or an older adult with heart failure, diabetes, new home oxygen, and no family nearby?
check.a: The older adult. Several chronic illnesses, new equipment, many providers, and little support create the greatest need for coordination.

sections.heading: What does access to care mean?
sections.keyIdea: Access means getting in, getting to a site with the service, and finding a provider the client can trust.
sections.body:
The Institute of Medicine (IOM) describes access as three steps. A client can pass one step and fail the next. A client with new Medicaid may find no nearby clinic taking new Medicaid patients. That is a step 2 failure.

Uneven distribution also blocks step 2. Rural areas lack specialists; an obstetrician may be 100 miles away. Cities may face poverty and language barriers. RNs and NPs cluster in the eastern U.S.
steps: Step 1 — Gain entry into the system, usually through insurance or a safety-net program.
Step 2 — Reach a site of care that offers the needed services.
Step 3 — Find a provider the client can talk to, trust, and get individual needs met by.
bullets: COVID-19 showed disparities. The Navajo Nation had the highest per-capita rate in the U.S. early on.
Causes: no running water, high diabetes and hypertension rates, food deserts with long trips to crowded stores, little internet for telehealth.
Also high risk: essential workers, crowded homes, transit riders, nursing home and prison residents.

sections.heading: Who is uninsured, underinsured, or covered?
sections.keyIdea: Match the client to the right safety net, and remember EMTALA guarantees emergency screening regardless of ability to pay.
sections.body:
Uninsured people have no coverage. Rates are higher among minorities, low-wage and small-business workers, the unemployed, and the self-employed. They face delayed care, medical debt, and worse outcomes. Underinsured people have coverage that falls short. Both may ration care in ways that look like nonadherence.

Uninsured rates fell after the 2010 ACA, then rose. Causes include the end of the mandate penalty, non-ACA plans that exclude preexisting conditions, rules for noncitizens, and lower Medicaid enrollment.

rows: Older adult; dialysis client of any age
Low income; services Medicare lacks, such as long-term nursing home care
Children above Medicaid income limits; pregnant women in some states
“We make too much for Medicaid” + child
Health departments and community health centers
Uninsured client in the ED or in labor

sections.example: SAFETY ALERT—EMTALA. An uninsured client in active labor arrives at the ED. The clerk suggests sending her elsewhere. The hospital must give a screening exam regardless of ability to pay. Because she is in labor, it must stabilize her (generally delivery) or arrange a proper transfer. Payment questions never delay screening.

check.q: A client’s plan does not cover her diabetes medicine. Uninsured or underinsured?
check.a: Underinsured. Ask if she is rationing doses and involve social work.

sections.heading: Why does a usual source of care matter?
sections.keyIdea: A regular provider builds trust and prevention, so link every client who lacks one to a medical home.
sections.body:
Perceptions of need shape when people seek care. Some wait too long with chest pressure. Others use the ED for minor problems. In Clinical Example A, a parent brings a child to the ED 15 minutes after giving acetaminophen for an earache. Teach home care, drug onset time, and when to use primary, urgent, or emergency care—with respect.

More than 40 million Americans lack a usual source of care. Ask, “Who do you see for checkups?” If “nobody,” link them to a medical home. Box 46.2 lists its six principles.
bullets: A personal provider who leads care.
A provider-directed practice team.
Whole-person care across all life stages.
Coordinated, integrated care across the system and community.
Quality and safety through EBP, decision support, and measurement.
Enhanced access (open scheduling, longer hours, secure messaging) and supportive payment.
Separate list—AHRQ’s five features: patient-centered, comprehensive, coordinated, accessible, committed to quality and safety.

check.q: Which practice best fits PCMH: seeing whoever is open, clients arranging their own referrals, or open scheduling with evening hours and secure messaging?
check.a: Open scheduling, evening hours, and messaging—enhanced access. The others break the personal-provider and coordination principles.

sections.heading: Common traps: care models and coverage
sections.keyIdea: Find the defining clue—money, coordination, or client wishes; no coverage or weak coverage; age or income.
sections.body: Use the clue in the right column.

rows: Networks and cost for groups vs arranging services for one complex client.
Coordination process vs client wishes shaping the plan.
“Needs a referral” = HMO. “Self-refers, pays more” = PPO.
No plan vs a plan that excludes needed drugs or vaccines.
Age 65+ or disability vs low income. Long-term nursing home care = Medicaid.
“Earns too much for Medicaid” + child = CHIP.
EMTALA guarantees screening and stabilization, not free ongoing care.
Perception of need vs uneven distribution
ED for a minor issue = perception. Specialist 100 miles away = distribution.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The best answer fixes the barrier with respect; drop options that blame the client or offer a short-term workaround.
sections.body: Look for these common patterns in access questions.
bullets: Best response to a cost or access barrier.
Referral choice: who goes to the case manager, or which program fits.
EMTALA: what the ED must do for a client who cannot pay.
Safety first: stopped BP pills for cost with BP 172/104? Assess for headache, chest pain, vision change, and neuro deficits before referring.
sections.example: Sample question: A parent brings a 4-year-old to the ED for ear pain. Acetaminophen was given 15 minutes ago. The child is afebrile and playing. The parent says, “We don’t have a regular doctor.” After screening shows the child is stable, what is best? A. Tell the parent the ED is for emergencies only. B. Explain acetaminophen’s onset and help set up a primary care provider. C. Give a second dose now. D. Use urgent care for all future illness.
steps: Read the stem: the child is stable after screening, so EMTALA is met.
What is it asking? The action that fixes the underlying access problem.
Key cues: dose given 15 minutes ago (perception of need) and no regular doctor (no usual source of care).
A is judgmental. C risks overdose. D still leaves no medical home.
The answer is B. It addresses both cues.
Strategy: pick the answer that respectfully fixes the barrier.

sections.heading: Worked case: uninsured client with chest pain
sections.keyIdea: Screen and stabilize first; talk about cost and access only after the client is safe.
sections.body: Ms. Greene, 49, is a self-employed house cleaner with no insurance. She comes to a small rural ED with chest pressure on and off for two days. She says, “I waited because I can’t pay. Can you just give me something?” The nearest cath lab is 70 miles away. She stopped her BP pills when they got too expensive. She has no primary provider.
steps: Cues: possible acute coronary syndrome, no insurance, delayed care for cost, stopped BP pills, no usual source of care, rural distance.
Safety: EMTALA requires a screening exam regardless of ability to pay. Get a 12-lead ECG promptly per protocol and vital signs, and notify the provider.
Reassure: “Your health comes first. We’ll talk about costs after we know you are safe.”
If the hospital cannot treat her emergency, stabilize and arrange a proper transfer to the cath lab facility.
Plan access: social work for Medicaid or marketplace options, financial help, a sliding-fee clinic as her medical home, generic BP pills.
Teach: chest pain means call 911, whatever the cost.

check.q: The registration clerk asks Ms. Greene for a deposit before she is seen. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Step in so the screening exam happens without delay. EMTALA bars delaying screening or stabilization to ask about payment. Use the chain of command if needed.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: NC law lets minors consent to some services, which can remove a major access barrier for teens.
bullets: Minor consent (G.S. 90-21.5): a minor may consent to care for sexually transmitted and other reportable diseases.
Also pregnancy care (prevention, diagnosis, treatment)—but not sterilization or abortion.
Also abuse of controlled substances or alcohol, and emotional disturbance.
Emancipated minors may consent to their own care. The age of majority is 18.
Disabled adults (G.S. 108A-102): anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to county DSS. Good-faith reporters are immune.
Telehealth: NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. The NC Board of Nursing regulates practice under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Module 46 study guide, outcomes 46.3–46.4; textbook pp. 2777–2780 (Clinical Examples A and B, EMTALA Safety Alert, Box 46.2). Cases and walkthroughs are original.
The source says the ACA individual mandate was “repealed.” Technically, the federal penalty dropped to $0 in 2019; the effect on enrollment is the same.
Medicaid’s nursing home coverage means long-term custodial care. Medicare covers only limited, short-term skilled nursing care after a qualifying hospital stay.
Medicare covers people of any age with end-stage renal disease.
HMOs cover emergency care even out of network.
Premium, copay, deductible, and case-management steps were added as standard content.

mnemonics.name: Three frameworks: “Money, Map, Me”
mnemonics.text: Managed care = MONEY (cost and quality for groups). Case management = MAP (the route across settings). Patient-focused care = ME (the client’s needs lead).

mnemonics.name: EMTALA = “Screen, Stabilize, Safely Send”
mnemonics.text: Everyone who asks gets a screening exam. An emergency or active labor must be stabilized. Transfer only when appropriate—never because the client cannot pay.

pearls: Discharge planning, including case management referral, begins on admission.
Payment questions must never delay an ED screening exam.
Underinsured clients often look nonadherent. Ask about drug cost and coverage.
CHIP fills the gap for children whose families earn too much for Medicaid.
Respond to ED overuse with teaching and a medical home, not judgment.
The competent client leads decisions; family are partners when the client wishes.
redFlags: Any delay in an ED screening exam to check insurance or collect payment.
A client who stopped a critical drug (BP pill, insulin, anticonvulsant, anticoagulant) for cost. Assess, notify the provider, and involve social work.
A client who delayed care for chest pain, stroke signs, or heavy bleeding because of cost. Treat as an emergency first.
A rural pregnant client far from obstetric care with signs of labor or complications. Plan timely transport.

checks.q: A client with type 1 diabetes says, “My plan doesn’t cover my insulin brand, so I’ve been using half doses.” How should the nurse respond?
checks.a: She is underinsured and rationing insulin. Check glucose and for signs of diabetic ketoacidosis, notify the provider, and involve case management.

checks.q: A family earns slightly too much for Medicaid and cannot afford private insurance for their 7-year-old. Which program fits?
checks.a: CHIP, the Children’s Health Insurance Program.

checks.q: A rural client at 26 weeks lives 100 miles from the nearest obstetrician. What helps?
checks.a: The barrier is uneven distribution of services. Help with transport, use telehealth where suitable, coordinate with a closer clinic, and teach warning signs and a labor travel plan.

checks.q: An older adult on Medicare with very low income needs long-term custodial nursing home care. Which program likely pays?
checks.a: Medicaid. Medicare covers only limited, short-term skilled nursing care.

checks.q: After teaching about ED use for ear pain, which parent statement shows understanding?
checks.a: “I’ll give the medicine time to work and call our new clinic if the pain continues.” It shows drug-onset knowledge and use of a usual source of care.

topics.title: Care Delivery Models, Delegation & Resource Allocation
topics.summary: Compare functional, team, and primary nursing, delegate safely within a team, and allocate scarce resources by clinical need while advocating for fair care.
objectives: You can tell functional, team, primary nursing, and total patient care apart.
You can describe what the RN team leader and the associate nurse do.
You can use the five rights to decide what to delegate to UAP and LPNs.
You can explain the trade-offs of decentralized nursing workstations.
You can name why U.S. healthcare costs keep rising.
You can tell allocation from rationing and allocate by clinical need.
topics.bigPicture:
Every unit has a nursing care delivery model. It is the plan for who cares for which clients and how work is divided. You may notice it only when it changes. In a snowstorm, the charge nurse may say, “You pass all the meds, and the aides do baths.” That is functional nursing.

Delivery models set up the NCLEX’s favorite management questions. What can the RN delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)? Which client goes to the licensed practical nurse (LPN)? The rule never changes. The RN delegates tasks but keeps accountability. Beds, staff, and money are limited too, so nurses must share them fairly.
recap: Functional nursing divides work by task. It is efficient in emergencies but fragmented and impersonal.
Team nursing is most common. The RN team leader stays responsible for every client on the team.
Primary nursing gives one RN 24/7 accountability from admission to discharge; an associate nurse follows the plan.
Delegate tasks, never the nursing process. Assess, plan, teach, and evaluate stay with the RN.
Five rights of delegation: task, circumstance, person, direction, supervision. If one fails, do not delegate.
Decentralized pods increase bedside time but need planned communication to keep teamwork.
Rationing limits beneficial care because there is not enough. Allocate by clinical need, never status or ability to pay.

keyTerms.def: How a unit divides nursing work and client assignments, who holds authority and accountability, and how care is coordinated.
Task-based care used in shortages or emergencies. The charge nurse gives each person tasks, not clients. Efficient but fragmented.
The most common model. An RN team leader is responsible for all team clients and directs RNs, LPNs, and UAP.
Relationship-based care. One primary nurse has 24/7 authority and responsibility for a group of clients from admission to discharge.
In primary nursing, the nurse who follows the primary nurse’s plan on the primary nurse’s days off and reports needed changes.
One RN gives all care to a group of clients for one shift. Continuity ends with the shift. (Not detailed in the course source.)
Unlicensed helpers (may be certified) who assist with ADLs and basic care under licensed-nurse direction.
Giving a competent person the authority to do a specific nursing task, while the RN keeps accountability for the outcome.
Giving work that is already within the person’s own scope, such as an RN giving a stable client to an LPN.
Being answerable for your actions, including the decision to delegate and the follow-up.
Small charting stations in pods near client rooms, instead of one central station.
Ordering tests mainly to avoid lawsuits, not because the client needs them. It raises costs.
Sharing limited resources among competing needs. Macroallocation happens at policy level; microallocation happens at the bedside.
Limiting helpful care because there is not enough for all. Explicit uses stated rules; implicit happens through waits, costs, or shortages.
Sharing benefits and burdens fairly, by need, without regard to social worth, ability to pay, or traits unrelated to need.

sections.heading: What are the nursing care delivery models?
sections.keyIdea: Functional divides by task, team by client group, and primary by relationship—each trades cost against continuity.
sections.body:
A delivery model answers three questions. Who is assigned to the client? Who holds authority and accountability? How is the work divided?

Functional nursing splits work by task. It needs fewer RNs, so it returns in shortages and emergencies. But no one sees the whole client. A client who is more confused at 1400 than at 0900 can be missed. Clients may not know which nurse is theirs.

Team nursing splits work by client group under an RN leader. Primary nursing ties one RN to the client for the whole stay. It gives the most continuity but needs more RNs.

rows: RN leader directs RNs, LPNs, UAP for a client group
Individualized care; RNs do complex work
One RN gives all care for one shift

sections.example: A snowstorm leaves a 30-bed unit with two RNs, one LPN, and two UAP. The charge nurse switches to functional nursing. Each person takes a task type. Short huddles at 1000 and 1400 help someone still see each whole client.

check.q: A nurse manager of an oncology unit with long stays wants better continuity and has budget for more RNs. Which model fits?
check.a: Primary nursing. One RN follows each client from admission to discharge. Its main drawback, cost, is covered by the budget.

sections.heading: What do team leaders and primary nurses do?
sections.keyIdea: The team leader stays responsible for every team client; the associate nurse follows the primary nurse’s plan and reports changes.
sections.body:
The RN team leader keeps responsibility for every team client, even when tasks are delegated. The RN keeps unstable, new, complex, and teaching clients. LPNs take stable clients with predictable outcomes. UAP do activities of daily living (ADLs), walking, positioning, intake and output (I&O), and routine vital signs on stable clients.

In primary nursing, the primary nurse assesses on admission, writes the plan, and stays accountable through discharge. On days off, an associate nurse follows the plan. If a change is needed, the associate acts for safety and tells the primary nurse.
steps: Take handoff and find unstable or high-risk clients first.
Match clients to staff by acuity, skill, and scope.
Give specific directions: what, when, and what to report.
Check in at set times, evaluate, and reassign if a client changes.
sections.example: On the primary nurse’s day off, a transplant client develops mouth sores. The associate nurse starts the mouth-care protocol and tells the primary nurse, who updates the plan.

check.q: A UAP reports, “Mr. Patel’s oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. It was 95% this morning.” What does the RN do first?
check.a: Go assess Mr. Patel: airway, breathing, lung sounds, and vital signs. The UAP collects data, but interpreting and acting on it is the RN’s job.

sections.heading: How do I delegate safely?
sections.keyIdea: The RN can hand off a task but never the accountability or the nursing judgment.
sections.body:
Delegation gives a competent person authority to do a task. The RN keeps accountability for the choice and for follow-up. Assignment gives work already within the person’s scope, such as a stable client to an LPN.

The RN never delegates initial assessment, judgment, care planning, initial or new teaching, evaluation, or care of unstable clients. LPNs collect data, reinforce teaching, and care for stable clients under RN or provider supervision. Test every choice with the five rights. If one fails, do not delegate.

rows: Is it routine, standard, and judgment-free?
Discharge teaching given to a UAP
Is the client stable? Is help available?
UAP walks a client who just became dizzy
Is it in their scope, job list, and proven skill?
Sterile dressing given to an aide without it on her list
Did I say exactly what, when, and what to report?
“Check on Mr. Lee” instead of “BP at 1000; tell me if systolic is under 100”
Will I follow up and evaluate?

check.q: For a stable postop client, which can go to a UAP: measuring I&O, assessing the incision, walking in the hall, teaching incentive spirometry, vital signs?
check.a: I&O, walking, and vital signs. Incision assessment and teaching need the RN; the UAP may later remind the client to use the spirometer.

sections.heading: How do systems link to other nursing concepts?
sections.keyIdea: Unit design is an EBP example: decentralized pods add bedside time, but teamwork needs planned communication.
sections.body:
Decentralized workstations split a large unit into pods with charting stations near rooms and supplies. Research shows less walking, more time with clients, and higher client satisfaction. But nurses may feel isolated and report lower teamwork.

This is how evidence-based practice works in systems. One outcome improves while another gets worse. Do not scrap the design. Add planned communication: huddles, pod buddies, mobile devices, and visual help signals.

The table shows how healthcare systems connect to other nursing concepts.

rows: Team leader follows up on every delegated task
Pushing for an interpreter or financial counseling
Giving a scarce bed by need, not insurance
ACA, Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, EMTALA; writing legislators
EMTALA, scope of practice, delegation rules
Tracking readmissions after a new discharge process
Reporting unsafe staffing through the chain of command

check.q: After a switch to pods, nurses feel isolated and slow to get help during a fall. Best action?
check.a: Add planned communication—pod buddies, huddles, mobile alerts—instead of returning to a central station.

sections.heading: Why do healthcare costs keep rising?
sections.keyIdea: Costs rise from longevity, chronic disease, technology, and demand; nurses cut waste and harm, never needed care.
sections.body:
U.S. per-capita health spending reached $10,739 in the year the course cites. Recent federal figures are higher. Hospital care is the largest share.

Good cost control removes waste and prevents harm. Delaying pain medicine or turning clients less often is unsafe, not cost control.
bullets: People live longer, often with several chronic illnesses.
Chronic disease is rising, such as obesity-related diabetes.
Expensive new drugs, imaging, devices, and robotic surgery.
Consumer demand for the newest tests.
Defensive medicine—tests ordered to avoid lawsuits.
Insured clients are shielded from true costs.
Direct-to-consumer drug and specialty advertising.
sections.example: Safe cost control on a unit: remove urinary catheters and IVs as soon as they are not needed. Start discharge planning on admission. Use teach-back to prevent readmissions. Open supply kits only when needed. Prevent falls, pressure injuries, CAUTI, and CLABSI, which add days and cost.

sections.heading: How are scarce resources shared fairly?
sections.keyIdea: Allocate by clinical need and risk of harm—never by status, insurance, race, disability, or personality.
sections.body:
Resource allocation is sharing limited resources among competing needs. Macroallocation happens at policy level, like Medicaid rules or ICU bed counts. Microallocation happens at the bedside, like who gets the one sitter.

Rationing limits helpful care because there is not enough. Explicit rationing uses stated rules, like organ allocation or crisis standards. Implicit rationing hides in waits, costs, and shortages. One child psychiatrist for a region, with 4-month waits, is rationing. It hurts vulnerable groups most.

Use justice, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and autonomy. In disasters, utility—the most good for the most people—leads.
steps: Gather objective data on each client’s need, acuity, and likely benefit.
Apply the stated criteria or triage protocol.
Remove bias: ability to pay and status do not count.
Escalate when needs exceed resources; document and consult ethics if needed.

check.q: One ICU bed is open: a DKA client whose anion gap closed, a COPD client at baseline SpO2 90%, a septic client with mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 58 after a 30 mL/kg bolus, or a board member with normal troponins. Who gets it?
check.a: The septic client—shock after fluids means the highest risk. Status never moves a client up.

sections.heading: Common traps: models, delegation, and allocation
sections.keyIdea: Watch the verbs and the stability words—they tell you who does the task.
sections.body: Use the clue in the right column.

rows: Split by task vs split by client group. “One nurse gives all meds” = functional.
Daily assignments vs one RN for the whole stay. “Associate nurse” = primary.
Primary nursing vs total patient care
24/7 for the stay vs one shift only.
Primary nursing vs primary care vs primary prevention
A delivery model vs a setting vs a prevention level.
Task to UAP (RN keeps accountability) vs work within the person’s scope.
LPN reinforces. RN does all new teaching.
Sharing limited resources vs some people go without helpful care.
Removing an unneeded catheter vs skipping needed care.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Circle the verb and the stability word; the delegable answer is routine, standard, and on a stable client.
sections.body: Expect items on naming a model, delegating, accountability, and scarce resources.
bullets: Unsafe staffing: accept, prioritize, and escalate through the chain of command. Walking off is abandonment.
Accountability: “Once I delegate, I’m no longer accountable” always needs more teaching.
Direction: name the time, method, what to report, and by when. “Use your judgment” is too vague.
sections.example: Sample question: An RN team leader works with an LPN and a UAP. Which task is best to delegate to the UAP? A. Assess the skin of a client admitted with a stage 2 pressure injury. B. Help a client with stable chronic heart failure walk to the bathroom. C. Teach a client newly diagnosed with diabetes to check glucose. D. Monitor a client who returned from cardiac catheterization 30 minutes ago.
steps: Read the stem: it asks what the UAP can safely do.
What is it asking? A routine task on a stable client.
Key cues: “assess,” “teach,” “newly diagnosed,” and “30 minutes ago” signal RN work.
A needs RN skin assessment. C is new teaching. D is a high-risk post-cath client.
The answer is B, a routine ADL for a stable client.
Strategy: assess, teach, evaluate = RN. New, just returned, unstable = RN.

sections.heading: Worked case: team leader on a short night
sections.keyIdea: See the unstable client first, keep RN-only work, delegate routine tasks with clear directions, and speak up for staff.
sections.body: You lead a surgical team at 1900 with one LPN and one nursing assistant. A float RN is offered, but the supervisor asks if you can manage. Your clients are listed below.
steps: Cues: Mr. E is unstable, Ms. B is new, Ms. D needs new teaching. Mr. A and Mr. C are stable.
See Mr. E first. Assess breathing and vital signs, give oxygen per protocol, and notify the provider.
Keep Mr. E, Ms. B, and Ms. D. Assign Mr. A and Mr. C to the LPN.
Delegate walking, hygiene, vital signs, and I&O to the aide. Say what to report, like SpO2 under 92%.
Accept the float RN and explain why. Advocating for safe staffing is a duty.

check.q: The LPN offers to do Ms. D’s first ostomy teaching so you can focus on Mr. E. Best response?
check.a: Decline that task—initial teaching is the RN’s job. The LPN can reinforce it later.

bullets: Mr. A: day 2 after bowel surgery, stable.
Ms. B: admitted an hour ago with bowel obstruction, NG tube, IV fluids.
Mr. C: day 3 after knee replacement, stable.
Ms. D: new colostomy; needs ostomy teaching.
Mr. E: SpO2 fell from 95% to 89% in the last hour.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, a task must be on the aide’s approved list and safe for this client right now before the RN delegates it.
bullets: The NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).
RN rules: 21 NCAC 36 .0224. LPN rules: 21 NCAC 36 .0225.
The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. The LPN works under RN or provider supervision.
The RN delegates tasks, not the nursing process. NCBON publishes a “Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP” and a scope-of-practice decision tree.
Nurse Aide I registry: NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. Nurse Aide II registry: NCBON; must also be on the NA I registry.
NA II tasks include some sterile tasks, like sterile dressings and oxygen. A listed task is not automatically safe for an unstable client.
Just Culture: NCBON’s Complaint Evaluation Tool sorts events into human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior.
Diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches go to the Board. NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state; follow the law where the client is.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Module 46 study guide, outcomes 46.5–46.7; textbook pp. 2780–2782. Page 2782 was partly illegible; rationing definitions are on p. 2783.
Macro/microallocation, explicit/implicit rationing, and distributive justice are standard ethics content added to fill that gap.
The $10,739 figure matches 2017 U.S. data. Recent CMS figures exceed $14,000 per person. Hospital care is still the largest share.
In functional nursing, the charge nurse technically assigns tasks within scope and delegates to UAP.
Total patient care and the five rights were added as standard NCLEX content.
“Team nursing is the most frequently used model” is from the course; many hospitals blend it with total patient care.
The course says the team leader “delegates” to RNs and LPNs. Under NCSBN/ANA guidelines, work within a person’s scope is assignment. The leader stays accountable either way.

mnemonics.name: Delivery models: “Task, Team, Tie”
mnemonics.text: Functional = TASK (split by job). Team = TEAM (RN leader plus a client group). Primary = TIE (one nurse tied to the client, admission to discharge, 24/7).

mnemonics.name: Never delegate to UAP: “EAT” + unstable
mnemonics.text: Evaluate, Assess, Teach—plus any unstable or unpredictable client. These stay with the RN.

pearls: The team leader stays responsible for all team clients, including delegated tasks.
Unstable, new, or unpredictable clients belong to the RN.
A task on an aide’s list still needs the RN’s judgment that it is safe for this client now.
Cost control removes waste and prevents complications; it never withholds needed care.
redFlags: A UAP reports new low BP, low SpO2, or confusion. The RN assesses now.
Being asked to delegate a task outside an aide’s list or skill. Refuse and reassign.
Unsafe staffing for acuity. Escalate objectively through the chain of command and document.
Allocation swayed by ability to pay, race, disability, or status. Advocate and escalate.

checks.q: An NA II has proven skill in sterile dressings. Your client’s wound just opened and is draining heavily. Delegate the dressing?
checks.a: No. The client changed and needs RN assessment, so the circumstance right fails.

checks.q: During functional nursing, the med nurse notices a client is more lethargic but assumes the “assessment nurse” knows. What weakness is this?
checks.a: Fragmentation. Report the change to the responsible RN right away.

checks.q: Which client is best for the LPN: GI bleed, type 2 diabetes, new colostomy, or packed RBC transfusion?
checks.a: The stable client with type 2 diabetes. The others need RN assessment, new teaching, or close monitoring.

checks.q: An RN team leader says, “Once I delegate a task to the aide, I am no longer accountable for it.” Correct?
checks.a: No. The RN stays accountable for the decision to delegate and for supervising and evaluating the result.

checks.q: Two clients need the last telemetry bed: new chest pain with ECG changes, or stable atrial fibrillation with anxiety. Who gets it?
checks.a: The client with new chest pain and ECG changes—greatest need and risk.

checks.q: An LPN is assigned a stable client with diabetes. What teaching may the LPN do?
checks.a: Reinforce teaching the RN already gave, like foot care. The RN does initial teaching and evaluates.
